data.question: Should we adopt the rule change hold_limit 70s → 80s, raise the constitutional floor min_company_on_time_rate from 0.6 to 0.65, or keep the current rules (v3) unchanged?
data.background: The hold_limit change improves the main goal (utility_gap narrows by +1.6, with 4/5 seeds improved), but it lowers the watched goal min_company_on_time_rate from 0.97 to 0.94. Trading the main goal against a watched goal is a KPI conflict, and your K5 reasoning says such trade-offs are decided case by case. R1 changes a value in the constitution, which is a regulation, so only humans may decide it, even though the current rules already meet the new floor.

options.summary: hold_limit rises from 70s to 80s. The gap between company utilities narrows by +1.6, and the result improves in 4/5 seeds. Utility A / B / C moves from 26.8 / 25.6 / 11.2 to 26.0 / 25.2 / 12.0. On-time deliveries fall from 85.6 to 85.0 and late deliveries rise from 1.8 to 2.4. The lowest on-time rate falls from 0.97 to 0.94, which still meets the KPI condition of 0.7. Blocked seconds rise from 976 to 1111. Road violations fall from 27.2 to 25.6, and sanction_total falls from 22.0 to 21.8. The vote is A ×, B ○, C ○, and the change passes both the check and the constitution.
options.stakeholders: C gains (+0.8 utility) and moves closer to the others, which supports the cooperation goal. A loses the most (−0.8) and voted against. B loses slightly (−0.4) but voted for the change. Customers lose a little: about 0.6 fewer on-time deliveries and 0.6 more late deliveries per period, plus more time blocked on the road. One company's on-time rate drops to 0.94.

options.summary: The constitutional floor min_company_on_time_rate rises from 0.6 to 0.65. The current rules (lowest rate 0.97) already meet it, so nothing changes now. Future rule proposals that push any company below 0.65 would be rejected automatically. The operational KPI condition stays at 0.7. This option can be decided independently of option 1.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain a stronger permanent guarantee that no company's service falls far behind. Companies lose some room to propose rules that trade a weak company's on-time rate for other gains, especially in a future busy season. No company's utility changes now.

options.summary: Stay at v3. Utility A / B / C stays 26.8 / 25.6 / 11.2, on-time deliveries stay 85.6, late deliveries stay 1.8, and the lowest on-time rate stays 0.97. The utility gap stays where D5 left it.
options.stakeholders: A keeps its current utility, and customers keep the slightly better on-time results. C remains far behind A and B, which works against the KPI aim that no company gains or loses because of how the road is used.

recommendation.reason: Option 1 serves the current main goal: it narrows the gap by +1.6, improves in 4/5 seeds, and keeps the lowest on-time rate at 0.94, well above the 0.7 condition. Its cost to customers (+0.6 late deliveries) is similar in size to D5, which you accepted as almost no cost to on-time delivery. Road violations and sanctions also fall slightly. R1 changes nothing now, and you chose in D1 and K5 to wait until the quiet season has been measured, so it can be deferred and decided separately.

unknowns: Why A voted against and whether A will change its behavior (for example, its routing or cooperation) if adopted against its vote
Which company's on-time rate drops to 0.94, and whether that company is C, the one this change is meant to help
How much the one seed that did not improve worsened, and how large the spread across seeds is
How customers perceive about 0.6 more late deliveries and longer blocked times per period
Next period's order volume, and whether the 80s hold_limit would hurt on-time delivery more when demand returns
Whether further increases to hold_limit would keep narrowing the gap or have reached diminishing returns
Whether a 0.65 constitutional floor would bind or block useful rules in a future busy season
